newsitem.title: UK: Kroto stunned by Nobel chemistry prize win.
newsitem.headline: Kroto stunned by Nobel chemistry prize win.

text.p: Britain's Sir Harold Kroto said on Wednesday he was stunned by the news that he and two U.S. scientists had won the 1996 Nobel Prize for Chemistry for their discovery of new forms of carbon.

"This is the greatest day of my life. It's fantastic. I'm about to have my first glass of champagne," he told Reuters by telephone from his office in the University of Sussex in southern England, where he is a professor of chemistry.
"A lot of great scientists don't even dream about this because the probability of winning it is beyond belief. I'm totally overwhelmed," said Kroto, 57.
"People had said it was a possibility so I knew it might be on the cards," he added, speaking loudly to drown out the noise of colleagues gathering to help him celebrate the win.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said Kroto, together with U.S. scientists Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, won the prize for their discovery in 1985 of fullerenes, new forms of carbon in which the atoms are arranged in closed shells.
"The element carbon had thus assumed an almost infinite number of different structures," the academy said.

Kroto said he had discovered the possible existence of fullerenes by chance as he and a team at the University of Sussex were carrying out an experiment to investigate the shape of carbon molecules found in stars.
He then contacted Curl and Smalley at Houston's Rice University, who confirmed his discovery.
"This opened up a vast area of chemistry for the 21st century. Fullerenes could be used in super-conductors and new kinds of compounds and drugs," Kroto said.
Before the discovery, scientists thought there were only two forms of pure carbon in existence -- normal carbon and diamonds.

The structure, shaped like a football, was called the "Buckminsterfullerene" after U.S. architect R. Buckminster Fuller, for his design of the geodesic dome at the 1967 Montreal World Expo. The dome closely resembles the chemical structure.
"Scientists should have discovered fullerenes 40 years ago but just didn't make the right calculations," said Kroto, who knows how he will spend his share of the $1.12 million prize.
"I work for a trust which has made five films explaining science to the general public in an unemotional way. I am looking to try to fill the deep debt this trust owes," he said.
